analysis.one_liner: Forces the Energy Department to decide natural gas export applications within 90 days.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan trio of Democratic senators' bill to speed up federal decisions on natural gas export permits never got a committee vote after being introduced in April 2014.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Energy to issue a decision on any application to export natural gas within 90 days of the close of the public comment period, and would have sent any legal challenge over an export decision — or over DOE failing to decide — to a single appeals court with fast-tracked handling and a 30-day deadline if the court found the department dragging its feet [S2] [S3]. Its practical effect would be to move natural gas export approvals out the door faster, limiting how long anyone can slow a project down through review or litigation [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers and companies seeking to build export terminals gain the most: a hard 90-day deadline plus fast-track court review means their permit applications cannot sit indefinitely at the Department of Energy, and challenges to approvals are steered into one expedited track [S2] [S3]. Some communities near export facilities could also see construction jobs, though the bill text contains no provisions aimed at them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Energy to decide any natural gas export application within 90 days after the end of the Federal Register comment period (or enactment of the bill), removing the department's ability to leave applications pending indefinitely.

Gives the federal appeals court in the region where the export facility would be built original and exclusive jurisdiction over challenges to export decisions — or to DOE's failure to decide — and requires expedited docketing of those cases.
Requires the court to order DOE to issue a decision within 30 days if it finds the department has failed to act on an application.

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses that buy natural gas. Exports increase demand for the same domestic supply, which tends to push up prices paid by American consumers and by manufacturers and utilities that use gas as a fuel or feedstock. The compressed 90-day clock also shortens the window for agencies and the public to weigh the effects of each export application before a decision is issued [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and businesses that use natural gas

drawbacks.text: A hard 90-day decision deadline compresses the review period for export applications, leaving less time to analyze how a project would affect domestic energy prices and the surrounding environment before approval.

Because exports raise demand for the same gas supply, faster approvals tend to lift domestic natural gas prices — a cost borne by ordinary households heating homes and by energy-intensive manufacturers that compete globally.
Routing all challenges to a single appeals court with expedited consideration narrows the opportunities for affected parties to contest an export approval in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real value to gas producers and export developers — certainty and speed on permits — but the costs would have fallen broadly on everyone who pays a gas bill or uses gas in manufacturing, through higher domestic prices, plus reduced time for public and interagency review. The benefits are concentrated in one industry while the costs are diffuse; on that arithmetic, the bill served a narrow commercial interest more than the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late April 2014, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Udall introduced the bill on April 30, 2014, joined by Sens. Mark Begich and Heidi Heitkamp.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.
No further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers of natural gas — households, manufacturers, and utilities — came out ahead, since the bill that would likely have pushed their prices up and shortened public review never advanced. The export industry gained nothing from the bill's death, but it had also lost nothing.

for.name: Sen. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 90-day deadline on natural gas export decisions and fast-track court review.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 30, 2014 and never held a markup or advanced it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never progressed far enough for a vote that would show how the parties lined up.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG export developers
industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed a decision on export applications within 90 days and fast-tracked any court challenge, removing the uncertainty that slows export projects. Its gains depend on shipping domestic gas abroad, which raises the domestic prices that households and manufacturers pay.

These industries burn natural gas as fuel or use it as a feedstock, so faster export approvals that push up domestic prices raise their costs — the same costs ordinary consumers face through utility bills and consumer prices.
Producers of all sizes benefit from a larger export market and firmer demand for domestically extracted gas.
